Architecture with mid-rise stucco and brick residential blocks, separated tram corridor, and street furniture also match German cities. While Cologne or Düsseldorf share some features, the overall look (narrower carriageway, older blocks, Ruhr-style corner shops) is very typical of Essen/Bochum/Dortmund. No landmark cleanly names the city, but the combination of tram alignment, building stock, and signage suggests Essen as a plausible candidate within North Rhine–Westphalia. Street level: The street curves gently left with a centerline broken marking, a tram stop platform and glass shelter on the left, and a distinctive rounded red-brick corner building with multiple shop signs just past the intersection. Tall grey catenary poles line the right verge, with small trees in a grassy strip and a separate sidewalk. A blue street sign sits beneath the bus-stop disk. These features could help match a specific corridor in Essen where trams run on a parallel reservation beside a two-lane carriageway and stops use the yellow H disk with platform shelters near a corner brick building.
